Herman Witsius
HUR-man WIT-see-us
proper noun (a Dutch Reformed theologian)
Hermann Wits, latinized Witsius (1636-1708); the Dutch Reformed theologian and covenant divine, author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.

See also: Herman Witsius

📖 Biblical Definition

Herman Witsius (1636-1708) was a Dutch Reformed theologian and one of the great covenant divines, best remembered for his masterwork The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man, a full and irenic exposition of the covenant of works and the covenant of grace. Learned, devout, and peaceable, he laboured to set forth the biblical covenants in their order and harmony, holding together the doctrines of grace with a warm experimental piety, and seeking to reconcile the more scholastic and the more pietistic strains of Reformed divinity in his day. The dictionary honours Witsius as a faithful expositor of covenant theology, which reads the whole of Scripture through the covenants God has made: the covenant of works with Adam, broken in the fall; and the covenant of grace in Christ, the second Adam, by which God promised, “I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed… to be a God unto thee.” This is the better covenant of which Christ is mediator, established upon better promises, the covenant under which God writes His law in the inward parts. Witsius rightly divided the word of truth, a workman approved unto God. The dictionary commends him as a model of Reformed covenant theology pursued with both precision and devotion—learning that warmed rather than chilled the heart—and as a witness that doctrinal exactness and experimental godliness are not rivals but companions. His Economy of the Covenants remains a standard exposition of the covenantal framework the Reformed tradition reads across the unity of Scripture, from the first Adam to the last.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Dutch Reformed covenant theologian (1636-1708), author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man; a model of covenant theology pursued with both doctrinal precision and warm experimental piety.

HERMAN WITSIUS, proper noun. [Hermann Wits, 1636-1708.] A Dutch Reformed theologian and covenant divine.

Author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.

A full, irenic exposition of the covenant of works and the covenant of grace.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the false divorce of doctrinal precision from experimental piety, which Witsius's life and work refute.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Witsius commends is the union of doctrinal precision and experimental godliness. A persistent error pits the two against each other—treating careful theology as cold and deadening, and warm piety as careless of doctrine. Witsius refutes the divorce. He was at once a precise covenant scholar and a man of devout, heartfelt religion, and he laboured to reconcile the scholastic and pietistic strains of the Reformed church of his day. The dictionary holds, with his example, that learning ought to warm the heart and that true devotion is built on sound doctrine.

Witsius also commends covenant theology itself as the framework for reading the unity of Scripture. The Bible is not a heap of disconnected stories but the unfolding of God's covenants—the covenant of works with Adam, broken in the fall, and the covenant of grace in Christ the last Adam, the better covenant established upon better promises. The dictionary commends Witsius as a faithful guide to this covenantal reading, and his Economy of the Covenants as a standard exposition, honouring him as a workman approved unto God who rightly divided the word of truth with both exactness and warmth.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Dutch Hermann Wits, latinized Witsius; a covenant theologian of the Dutch Further Reformation (Nadere Reformatie), expositor of the oikonomia (economy, ordered administration) of the covenants.

Hermann Wits (1636-1708), latinized “Witsius.”

A theologian of the Dutch Further Reformation (Nadere Reformatie).

The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man, his masterwork.

“Economy” (Greek oikonomia), the ordered administration of the covenants.

A model of covenant theology joined to experimental piety.
